title: Workspace occupancy and variance share
takeaway: Counted by sparse reconstruction, the J-space holds around 25 meaningfully active lens vectors per position in the median case — near zero in the early layers, a plateau across the workspace band — while explaining under 10% of activation variance beyond a random control. This is the paper's quantitative basis for calling the workspace capacity-limited: on the order of tens of concepts, and a small slice of what the model represents.
walkthrough:
The figure has two panels, both answering the same question: how much does the [[j-space]] actually hold? The first panel plots [[j-space-occupancy]] against layer depth. The second plots how much activation variance that occupied portion accounts for, at five workspace layers.

The occupancy metric works by reconstruction. At each position and layer, [[sparse-decomposition]] solves for a sparse nonnegative combination of $K$ [[j-lens-vector]]s that best reconstructs the [[residual-stream]] activation, using [[gradient-pursuit]]. Each added vector improves the reconstruction by some amount. The same procedure is run with a control set of random directions of the same size. Occupancy is the value of $K$ at which the marginal improvement from one more J-lens vector falls below the improvement from one more random direction. Past that point, the lens vectors are no better than chance, so the count stops there.

The first panel shows this count per layer, with lines for percentiles over positions rather than a single average. Occupancy is near zero through roughly the first third of the layers — the [[sensory-layers]], where the J-space carries essentially no content. It then rises to a plateau of around 25 in the median case, with the onset coinciding with the start of the [[workspace-layers]] identified by the paper's other boundary metrics. The value varies across contexts, which is what the percentile spread shows. Layers here follow the paper's [[layer-percentage-indexing]], so layer numbers read as percentages of depth.

The second panel fixes $K$ at each layer's median occupancy and measures [[excess-variance-explained]]: the fraction of activation variance the top-$K$ J-lens vectors capture beyond the same-size random control. This never exceeds 10%. The activations are dominated by information outside the J-space.

One caveat carries weight. Occupancy counts distinct active vectors, not concepts — the [[word-list-experiment]] shows that several related lens vectors can jointly represent one broader category. The paper therefore states its [[j-space-capacity]] claim at the order-of-magnitude level: tens of concepts at a time. At any single layer, the count of unrelated items is smaller still, around one or two.

terms.definition: The number of J-lens vectors meaningfully active in an activation: the value of $K$ at which the marginal reconstruction improvement from a sparse combination of $K$ J-lens vectors falls below that of a same-size random control set.
The number of J-lens vectors allowed in the sparse reconstruction. The first panel sweeps $K$ to find where the lens stops beating chance; the second panel fixes $K$ at each layer's median occupancy.

One direction in residual-stream space per vocabulary token per layer, identified by the Jacobian lens as encoding the model's disposition to say that token. The dictionary the reconstruction draws from.

A reconstruction of an activation as a weighted sum of at most $K$ J-lens vectors with all weights nonnegative, solved by gradient pursuit. The paper's operational way of listing what the J-space contains at a position.

A set of random directions of the same size as the J-lens set, run through the same reconstruction procedure. It fixes the baseline: any direction set explains some variance, so only improvement beyond this control counts.
Depth in the model, under the paper's convention of 25 evenly spaced layers reindexed 0-100, so layer numbers read as percentages of total depth.

The lines of the first panel: occupancy is computed per token position, and the figure shows percentile bands of its distribution across positions rather than one average curve, because the value varies across contexts.
The second panel's vertical axis: the fraction of activation variance captured by the top-$K$ J-lens vectors minus the fraction captured by the same-size random control. It never exceeds 10%.
The per-layer median of the occupancy distribution, around 25 across the workspace band. The second panel evaluates variance explained with $K$ set to this value at each layer.

The five layers from the middle band at which the excess-variance measurement is shown — the range, roughly from a third of the way through the depth to shortly before the output, where the J-space carries workspace-like content.

The greedy sparse-approximation algorithm used to solve for the reconstruction: it adds one dictionary vector at a time, which is what makes the marginal improvement per added vector a measurable quantity.
The per-position activation vector the reconstruction targets: the running state each transformer layer reads from and writes to.

numbers.meaning: The median occupancy plateau across the workspace band: about 25 J-lens vectors are meaningfully active at a typical position, though the value varies across contexts. This is also why the paper typically caps the sparsity level defining the J-space at 25.

The depth range where occupancy stays near zero — the sensory band, where J-lens readouts carry essentially no meaningful content. The rise out of it coincides with the workspace onset the paper locates at roughly layer 38 on its 0-100 scale.

The ceiling on excess variance explained at every measured workspace layer, with $K$ at median occupancy. The paper reads this as the model's activations being dominated by information outside the J-space.
The number of workspace layers at which the second panel evaluates excess variance explained.

The paper's stated capacity of the workspace, deliberately loose: occupancy counts active vectors, not concepts, since several related vectors can jointly encode one category, so the claim is made at the order-of-magnitude level.

The number of unrelated list items simultaneously represented at any single layer, from the appendix's single-layer analysis — smaller than the ~25 figure, which pools the best rank over the whole workspace band.

The workspace band identified in section 4.1 by four lens-derived boundary metrics, on the 0-100 layer scale; the occupancy plateau spans this same band, which the paper takes as independent confirmation of the band.
The paper's layer-reporting convention: 25 evenly spaced residual-stream layers, reindexed so a layer number reads as a percentage of model depth.
